title: When AI agents become cyber capabilities
summary: A technical field guide to autonomous replication, adaptive malware, vulnerability reproduction, exploit progression, and measuring AI-agent capability without confusing a crash with compromise.
takeaways: Tool access, credentials, compute, and feedback loops matter as much as model size.
A crash is evidence of a trigger, not proof of arbitrary code execution or durable control.
Benchmarks must separate discovery, reproduction, exploitation, patch quality, and impact.
Defenses should constrain reachable actions and verify outcomes independently.
reviewNote: A defensive synthesis. Each result is tied to its cited setup; benchmark results do not establish that a capability is universally available in production. Diagrams are conceptual, not deployment instructions.

blocks.text: An agent is a model embedded in a loop: observe state, choose an action, invoke a tool, receive feedback, repeat. The harness determines reachable tools, credentials, time budget, network access, retries, and stopping rules. Therefore model capability alone is an incomplete threat model.

blocks.title: Agent control loop
blocks.note: Risk rises with broad permissions, persistent credentials, writable state, network reachability, and missing stop conditions. Verify outside the model's own narrative.

blocks.title: Security takeaway
blocks.text: Constrain the reachable action space even when model behavior is uncertain. Tool permissions and environment affordances can change practical capability dramatically.

METR's 2023 report defines autonomous replication and adaptation (ARA) as a cluster of abilities: acquiring resources, creating copies, and adapting to unfamiliar tasks. Its agents completed easier tasks and made progress on harder ones across 12 tasks; the authors cautioned that these evaluations could not rule out future capability gains.

Anthropic's October 12, 2026 research note reports that a 9B model got inference running on 8 of 9 hardware types tested, and says models of 30B parameters or less can complete many individual replication steps. Running inference on a device is not the same as end-to-end unauthorized replication, persistence, or uncontrolled spread.

blocks.caption: ARA decomposition and defensive evidence
rows: Obtain compute, accounts, or other resources
Identity and cloud audit logs; quota alerts
Create and launch a functioning copy
Workload lineage, artifact hashes, deployment records
Versioned action traces and controlled replay
Lifecycle telemetry, lease expiry, revocation tests

blocks.text: The adaptive-worm paper studies agent-generated, target-specific propagation strategies and the use of compromised machines as compute. The conceptual shift is from a fixed exploit strategy to a feedback-driven process, increasing the importance of segmentation, egress controls, identity isolation, and containment.

blocks.title: Defender's propagation-control loop
blocks.note: Defensive abstraction of the threat model; no exploit construction steps.

blocks.caption: Where to break the chain
rows: Prevent credential reuse and privilege expansion
Short-lived scoped tokens; privileged sign-in events
Limit lateral movement and outbound paths
East-west flow, DNS, proxy, firewall logs
Isolation drills, token revocation, egress blocks

sections.title: ExploitBench: exploitation is a ladder, not a boolean

blocks.text: ExploitBench argues that a crash-only benchmark hides the hard transitions between reaching vulnerable code, triggering a bug, building useful primitives, escaping a sandbox, hijacking control flow, and achieving arbitrary code execution. It evaluates 41 V8 bugs using 16 capability flags and deterministic checks.

blocks.title: High-level capability ladder
blocks.note: Each rung is a distinct outcome. Success at one rung does not prove a higher rung.

blocks.caption: What a result actually proves
rows: A compromise beyond the evaluated environment

blocks.text: The authors describe randomized challenge-response checks, differential execution against ground-truth binaries, and a signal-handler proof for code execution. Independent deterministic oracles make it harder for an agent to pass by producing plausible-looking artifacts or exploiting weak grading.

blocks.title: Benchmark principle
blocks.text: Report a capability vector c = (c₁, …, cₖ), with each cᵢ ∈ {0,1} representing an independently verified capability. Preserve target version, mitigations, harness, tool budget, and verifier for reproducibility.

CyberGym contains 1,507 benchmark instances across 188 software projects. In the primary task, an agent receives a vulnerability description and pre-patch codebase, then generates a proof-of-concept test. Success is checked against vulnerable and patched versions, rather than judging textual plausibility alone.

items.text: Benchmark instances derived from real vulnerability history.

items.title: Pre-patch / post-patch
items.text: Differential validation checks whether a PoC triggers before a fix and stops triggering after.

items.title: Open-ended discovery
items.text: Separate experiments scan current codebases and validate candidate crashes.

blocks.title: Vulnerability reproduction pipeline
blocks.note: A valid reproduction should trigger on the vulnerable version and not reproduce the same issue on the fixed version. False positives and incomplete fixes require triage.

blocks.text: CyberGym's website also reports open-ended scans across 431 OSS-Fuzz projects and confirmed zero-days and incomplete patches. Treat those as results of that follow-on methodology and validation process, not as a universal score for every agent. Live leaderboards can change over time.

blocks.title: Why differential testing matters
blocks.text: A single crash is noisy. Comparing vulnerable and patched builds helps distinguish a reproduced vulnerability from an unrelated failure, test-harness issue, or incomplete patch.

sections.title: Math for capability and risk analysis

items.title: Expected loss
items.text: Risk ≈ P(harmful event) × Impact. Condition probability on permissions, reachable assets, run duration, and controls.

items.title: Chain reliability
items.text: For n independent stages with success probabilities pᵢ: P(chain) = ∏ᵢ pᵢ. Independence is a simplifying assumption.

items.title: Observed success rate
items.text: p̂ = x / n, where x tasks pass a predefined oracle out of n attempts. Report sample size and task mix.

items.title: Approximate standard error
items.text: SE(p̂) ≈ √[p̂(1 − p̂) / n] under a simple binomial model. For small samples or extreme rates, consider Wilson intervals.

blocks.caption: Illustrative calculations, not reported paper results
rows: About 3.8 percentage points under simple assumptions
8% if these probabilities apply and independence is reasonable
Illustrative only; time horizons must match

blocks.text: These equations are analytical aids, not empirical laws. Agent stages are often correlated; benchmark tasks vary in difficulty; and stochastic runs may not be independent. A benchmark success rate is not automatically the probability of real-world compromise.

blocks.title: Don't let precision outrun evidence
blocks.text: Separate measured values, estimates, and illustrative inputs. Always state the task set, denominator, verifier, and uncertainty before comparing model scores.

sections.title: Blue-team controls: constrain, observe, verify, recover

blocks.caption: Practical control matrix
rows: Dedicated agent identity, narrow scopes, short-lived tokens
Can it read or change data outside its task?
Ephemeral workers, read-only mounts, restricted egress
Can it escape its intended filesystem or network zone?
Human approval for destructive changes and deployments
Does the approver receive evidence and have a real veto?
Structured tool logs, correlation IDs, immutable audit storage
Can responders reconstruct actions and results?
Action quotas, CPU/memory ceilings, timeouts, retry caps
Does it stop predictably when budget is exhausted?
Deterministic tests, policy checks, signed artifacts
Is success checked outside the agent's own narrative?
Revoke credentials, quarantine workloads, restore known-good state
Can the team stop the loop and prove recovery?

blocks.title: A safe deployment gate
blocks.note: Fail closed on policy violations. Approval only helps if the approver can understand and reject the proposed action.

blocks.text: Map AI-specific guardrails to established enterprise practices: identity governance, EDR, segmentation, vulnerability management, secure SDLC, change management, incident response exercises, and evidence retention. AI policy complements these controls; it does not replace them.

sections.title: How the five papers fit together

blocks.caption: Research comparison
rows: Can agents acquire resources, replicate, adapt?
Early task set cannot forecast all future systems.
Crash and code execution are different outcomes.
Can agents tailor propagation to hosts?
A demonstration is not proof every network is vulnerable.
How close are smaller models to device replication steps?
Subtasks do not prove uncontrolled end-to-end spread.

blocks.text: The shared direction is toward controlled, reproducible evaluations with real environments, independent oracles, and explicit capability tiers. The defensive response is to make dangerous actions unreachable by default, detect unexpected behavior, and preserve telemetry for rapid containment.

blocks.title: The right question
blocks.text: Capable of which action, against which target, with what permissions, under which mitigations, verified by what oracle, and at what rate across repeated trials?

glossary: Agent harness
Software connecting a model to tools, state, budgets, and stopping rules.
ARA
Autonomous replication and adaptation: resource acquisition, copying, and adapting to unfamiliar situations.
Proof of concept (PoC)
A test demonstrating a specific vulnerability behavior in a defined environment.
Differential testing
Comparing behavior across versions or configurations to isolate a change.
Oracle
An independent verifier for a predefined success condition.
Capability ladder
A set of increasingly consequential abilities rather than one binary score.
Lateral movement
Moving from an initially accessed system toward other systems or accounts.
Least privilege
Granting only the permissions needed for a task.
Sandbox escape
Crossing the security boundary of an isolated environment.
Egress control
A policy restricting outbound network connections.
False positive
An alert or test result that reports a condition that is not actually present.
